Voter ID is already required to register as a voter in California. All this proposition does is create another way for voters’ ballots to be thrown out in a state where almost 100,000 valid ballots were rejected (https://calvoter.org/content/making-sense-150000-rejected-california-mail-ballots) for arriving late in this year’s primary alone.
With a lawbreaking Riverside County sheriff and Republican gubernatorial candidate seizing ballots (https://berkeleypoliticalreview.org/2026/05/20/voting-rights-are-under-attack-california-must-stand-up-and-fight-back/) earlier this year, the last thing we need is to modify voting in this state. As usual, the only organizations on the “wrong side” of this proposition are the taxpayers’ associations. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association is in favor (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/) of this proposition passing because it would “secure” elections (i.e., make it harder to vote). This is fundamentally anti-democratic and should be opposed.
The “Billionaire Tax” Propositions:
YES on 40, NO on 41, NO on 42
These 3 propositions, which were put on the ballot by petition, are tied together. Prop. 40, possibly the most controversial (https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/californias-billionaire-tax-faces-mountain-opposition-not-just-rich-rcna604397) proposition of this election, would impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of California’s ~255 billionaires. Collectively, these high-wealth individuals hold over $2 trillion (https://www.oxfamamerica.org/explore/research-publications/billionaire-wealth-in-california/) (that’s two million millions) in total net worth.
Billionaires have fought tooth and nail to try to defeat Prop. 40. Mark Zuckerberg — perhaps California’s most iconic billionaire — has threatened to leave (https://www.bizjournals.com/sanfrancisco/news/2026/10/21/mark-zuckerberg-relocate-california-prop-40.html) the state if it passes. One might very well take this as an indication that Prop. 40 would be effective. And even if billionaires leave now, they will still have to pay the tax. Prop. 40 applies to anyone who was a California resident on January 1st (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-40) of this year.
The Voter Information Guide (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/quick-reference-guide/40.htm) says that Prop. 40 would raise tens of billions of dollars over several years, and that potential losses of income tax from billionaires relocating are estimated at less than $1 billion a year. This would be a net positive in terms of funds that would go to finance our streets, our schools, and our hospitals.
Even if Prop. 40 passes — as polling suggests (https://calmatters.org/newsletter/billionaire-tax-proposition-poll/) it might — Propositions 41 and 42 are aimed at undoing it. If either passes with more “yes” votes than Prop. 40, they will nullify its effects. Prop. 41 would nullify any new tax that exempts its revenue from California’s state spending limit (as the wealth tax proposed by Prop. 40 would). Prop. 42 would outright ban any wealth taxes in the state constitution.
Both of these reactionary propositions were funded by an organization that calls itself “Building a Better California” — which derives over half of its revenue (https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/29/politics/sergey-brin-california-wealth-tax) from Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who was willing to shell out $100 million from his quarter-trillion-dollar fortune in order to avoid paying a $14 billion tax.
Studies have suggested (https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2018/01/03/harvard-study-how-much-money-millionaires-need-to-be-happy.html) that human happiness maxes out at around an $8 million net worth. Perhaps any more than this only has negative repercussions on one’s personality.
Sergey Brin can afford to pay his fair share in order to support the state that facilitated his success. So can the rest of the over 250 billionaires that made their fortunes in California. Vote yes on Prop. 40, and no on Propositions 41 and 42.
Proposition 43: NO
This is an anti-democratic measure posing as fiscal responsibility. It should be opposed.
Prop. 43, very succinctly, would allow (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/) ⅓ of voters to veto the decisions of a ⅔ majority. Historically, special taxes in California have been able to pass with a simple majority (if they are proposed by citizens’ initiative rather than by city council members). These local measures are important for funding public transit, wildfire protection programs, and housing development.
The money-obsessed members of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association would like nothing more than to make these crucial taxes harder to pass, which is why (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/) they authored this proposition. Firefighters, teachers, and nurses all oppose Prop. 43. You should too.

While it may seem reasonable at first, this proposition is too extreme a solution for the problem it seems to combat. It should be voted against.
Prop. 44 would fine any community health clinic (a type of nonprofit health center) that spends less than 90% of its revenue on “program services” (direct clinical expenditures, as opposed to management and technology costs). Currently, clinics spend an average (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/analysis.htm) of about 80% of their revenue on these services. Disproportionately, community health clinics serve low-income and rural communities. This proposition passing would hurt members of these communities more than anyone else.

Proposition 45: NO
YIMBY (“Yes In My Backyard”) groups are largely not in favor of this seemingly progressive ballot measure. That’s one indicator that voting for it might not be a wise choice.
Prop. 45 would accelerate (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/) the timeline for environmental review of “essential” developments like housing and “broadband internet access” infrastructure, as well as require California courts to rule on California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) cases within 270 days (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-45-environmental-review/).

Conclusion
Of these fourteen propositions, the five most crucial ones to vote on (3, 40, 41, 42, and 43) all center around the extent to which money should be able to buy influence in politics. About $4.2 billion of this would almost certainly go (https://growsf.org/news/2026-07-02-14-state-measures/) to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, while the rest would fund research grants throughout the state. While the fact that this Institute’s founder is the primary bankroller of Prop. 38 may seem to reek of corruption, the benefits of this proposition still outweigh the costs.
Like Prop. 1, Prop. 38 would cost California hundreds of millions of dollars a year to pay off its debt, and like Prop. 1, these costs would be distributed over two decades. Alzheimer’s, heart disease, and cancer take millions of lives every year. Innovating solutions for them will help the entire world, not just Californian scientists.
Proposition 39: NO
Pushes to change Voter ID laws are politicized attacks on our democracy. They should be voted down.
Prop. 39 would require (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/) Voter ID at polling stations and, more significantly, would require all mail-in ballots (which 90% of Californians (https://calvoter.org/content/should-you-use-usps-mail-your-midterm-ballot-here%E2%80%99s-what-california-election-officials-say) use to vote) to be marked with the last four digits of a government ID number. Voter ID is already required to register as a voter in California. All this proposition does is create another way for voters’ ballots to be thrown out in a state where almost 100,000 valid ballots were rejected (https://calvoter.org/content/making-sense-150000-rejected-california-mail-ballots) for arriving late in this year’s primary alone.
With a lawbreaking Riverside County sheriff and Republican gubernatorial candidate seizing ballots (https://berkeleypoliticalreview.org/2026/05/20/voting-rights-are-under-attack-california-must-stand-up-and-fight-back/) earlier this year, the last thing we need is to modify voting in this state. As usual, the only organizations on the “wrong side” of this proposition are the taxpayers’ associations. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association is in favor (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/) of this proposition passing because it would “secure” elections (i.e., make it harder to vote). This is fundamentally anti-democratic and should be opposed.

YES on 40, NO on 41, NO on 42
These 3 propositions, which were put on the ballot by petition, are tied together. Prop. 40, possibly the most controversial (https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/californias-billionaire-tax-faces-mountain-opposition-not-just-rich-rcna604397) proposition of this election, would impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of California’s ~255 billionaires. Collectively, these high-wealth individuals hold over $2 trillion (https://www.oxfamamerica.org/explore/research-publications/billionaire-wealth-in-california/) (that’s two million millions) in total net worth.
Billionaires have fought tooth and nail to try to defeat Prop. 40. Proposition 43: NO
This is an anti-democratic measure posing as fiscal responsibility. It should be opposed.
Prop. 43, very succinctly, would allow (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/) ⅓ of voters to veto the decisions of a ⅔ majority. Historically, special taxes in California have been able to pass with a simple majority (if they are proposed by citizens’ initiative rather than by city council members). These local measures are important for funding public transit, wildfire protection programs, and housing development.
The money-obsessed members of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association would like nothing more than to make these crucial taxes harder to pass, which is why (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/) they authored this proposition. Firefighters, teachers, and nurses all oppose Prop. 43. You should too.
Proposition 44: NO
While it may seem reasonable at first, this proposition is too extreme a solution for the problem it seems to combat. It should be voted against.
Prop. 44 would fine any community health clinic (a type of nonprofit health center) that spends less than 90% of its revenue on “program services” (direct clinical expenditures, as opposed to management and technology costs). Currently, clinics spend an average (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/analysis.htm) of about 80% of their revenue on these services. YIMBY (“Yes In My Backyard”) groups are largely not in favor of this seemingly progressive ballot measure. That’s one indicator that voting for it might not be a wise choice.
Prop. 45 would accelerate (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/) the timeline for environmental review of “essential” developments like housing and “broadband internet access” infrastructure, as well as require California courts to rule on California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) cases within 270 days (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-45-environmental-review/).
A State Assembly bill written by housing-forward Assemblymember Buffy Wicks that streamlined CEQA was enacted (https://www.venable.com/insights/publications/2025/07/from-red-tape-to-green-light-ceqa-reforms-fast) last year (alongside a similar State Senate bill). Of these fourteen propositions, the five most crucial ones to vote on (3, 40, 41, 42, and 43) all center around the extent to which money should be able to buy influence in politics. Supporting 3 and 40 — and opposing 41, 42, and 43 — is the sensible position for those of us who believe in popular democracy; in fair, majority-wins elections; and in increased funding for our increasingly left-behind public schools and healthcare systems.

Affordable housing doesn’t pay for itself, but this proposition would help fund it.
Prop. 1 would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds: $10 billion for general affordable housing and $1.25 billion for veterans’ housing.

No formal arguments were filed against this proposition — only the infamously avaricious Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association objects (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/) to it.

The economic future of our state is not certain. This proposition would help us protect it.
Prop. 2 would double California’s existing Rainy Day Fund (which was approved (https://vigarchive.sos.ca.gov/2014/general/en/propositions/2/) by CA voters 12 years ago). The fund’s cap would be increased from 10% to 20% of the state budget, and the measure would mandate larger deposits during economic upturns.

This should be taken seriously, even if he claims it to be a joke. California should future-proof itself.
Partisan politics aside, saving more is often an economically sound decision. If we grow the Rainy Day Fund even further, we can prepare for the next recession. California’s revenue need not determine our quality of life.

Letting our income tax rates expire would cost California up to $15 billion (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/quick-reference-guide/3.htm) a year just to give tax cuts to high earners. This proposition would prevent that.

Might we not better spend our energy helping our underfunded public schools and hospitals?

While it may seem reasonable at first, this proposition is too extreme a solution for the problem it seems to combat. It should be voted against.

Currently, clinics spend an average (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/analysis.htm) of about 80% of their revenue on these services. If Prop. 44 passes, they would be required to pay exorbitant penalties, and, according to the California Primary Care Association, more than half may be forced (https://calmatters.org/newsletter/prop-44-medical-clinics/) to close. Disproportionately, community health clinics serve low-income and rural communities. This proposition passing would hurt members of these communities more than anyone else.
The labor union SEIU-UHW (Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West) is the main backer of Prop. 44. Most of SEIU-UHW’s members work at hospitals, not community clinics. The clinics potentially affected by Prop. 44 are largely non-union, and a coalition of them has alleged (https://www.legalnewsline.com/northern-california-record/union-uses-ca-ballot-initiatives-to-strongarm-clinics-lawsuit/article_7c623996-6763-48fc-88bf-65d50af60749.html) in a lawsuit that Prop. 44 serves as a bargaining chip for SEIU-UHW. They claim that the union offered to drop the proposition if union membership at community clinics increased.
Voting in favor of Prop. 44 is not in the public interest. There is a reason this proposition is opposed by Democrats and Republicans alike, as well as (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/) the California Medical Association. You should vote “no” on it.
Proposition 45: NO
YIMBY (“Yes In My Backyard”) groups are largely not in favor of this seemingly progressive ballot measure. That’s one indicator that voting for it might not be a wise choice.
Prop. 45 would accelerate (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/) the timeline for environmental review of “essential” developments like housing and “broadband internet access” infrastructure, as well as require California courts to rule on California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) cases within 270 days (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-45-environmental-review/).
A State Assembly bill written by housing-forward Assemblymember Buffy Wicks that streamlined CEQA was enacted (https://www.venable.com/insights/publications/2025/07/from-red-tape-to-green-light-ceqa-reforms-fast) last year (alongside a similar State Senate bill). But California YIMBY, which helped to write these reforms, declines to support (https://hoodline.com/2026/10/six-california-gop-county-committees-recommend-no-on-prop-45/) Prop. 45. It was placed on the ballot by the pro-business California Chamber of Commerce to “cut unnecessary delays” (https://advocacy.calchamber.com/alert/2026/07/voters-strongly-support-calchambers-prop-45) on development, while its opponents include the Coalition for Clean Air and CA Environmental Voters. Fundamentally, Prop. 45 is more than just a pro-housing measure. It could increase the likelihood (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/07/proposition-45-environment-health-protections/) of pollution in certain communities because it encourages rapid development, and its classification of “broadband internet access” development as being “essential” could fast-track data center construction, which 61% of Americans oppose (https://www.annenbergpublicpolicycenter.org/opposition-to-local-data-centers-rises-sharply-annenberg-survey-finds/). You should oppose this proposition as well.
Conclusion
Of these fourteen propositions, the five most crucial ones to vote on (3, 40, 41, 42, and 43) all center around the extent to which money should be able to buy influence in politics. Supporting 3 and 40 — and opposing 41, 42, and 43 — is the sensible position for those of us who believe in popular democracy; in fair, majority-wins elections; and in increased funding for our increasingly left-behind public schools and healthcare systems.

# Names Games and America’s Re-Frame: Trump’s Renaming Spree
By Molly Urfalian · May 2, 2025
My phone was constantly buzzing with “Breaking News” alerts during the first day of Trump’s presidency.
Seeing the flood of his executive orders, withdrawing the U.S. from the Paris Climate Agreement, the World Health Organization, eliminating DEI programs, and more was exhausting.
But I caught a break when I saw the headline reading “Trump renames ‘Gulf of Mexico’ to ‘Gulf of America’”.
...
After the initial shock faded, I had to ask: besides the fact that this was a hilarious move, why did he do it?
Well, he did not just rename the Gulf of Mexico; he has renamed a few geographical places around America.
Renaming the Gulf and “Mount Denali” is part of Trump’s Executive Order, “Restoring Names that Honor American Greatness.”
Unpacking these seemingly irrelevant changes and a few other examples reveals some patterns in Trump’s renaming frenzy.

PROP
4
REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Repeals prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns. Public funding programs may not use funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety. Fiscal Impact: Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs. Supporters: League of Women Voters of CA; California Nurses Association; Mental Health Advocacy; Social Security Works; Consumer Watchdog Opponents: California Taxpayers Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; Family Business Assn of California; United Latinos Action
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: State and local governments could create public campaign financing programs for public office candidates, subject to limits on which public funds could be used, how the public funds could be used, and who could receive them.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: State and most local governments would remain unable to create public campaign finance programs for public office candidates.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
YES ON 4. California is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns— communities in all other 49 states have this right. Special interests want to keep the ban to protect their power. Prop. 4 removes it. Strict taxpayer safeguards. Vote YES: Elections should be won, not bought.
CON
Prop. 4 allows politicians to use YOUR taxpayer money to fund their negative campaigns. Prop. 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money they can get. Worse yet, Prop. 4 allows SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY IN POLITICS. NO ON PROP. 4.

In Australia elections were frequently held in pubs because there were few public buildings.
The Returning Officer would have his table in one room.
The candidates would each occupy another room.
They were not charged for the room because the pub owner made his money from the food and drinks they had to lay on for their supporters and those who were voting for them.
A voter would go into the room of his chosen candidate.
Here there would be pen and paper as well as the food and drink.

PROP
4
REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Current law prohibits state and local governments from using public funds for election campaigns except in charter cities and counties.
This measure repeals that prohibition and allows state and local governments to establish public campaign financing programs for candidates who agree to specified spending limits and meet eligibility criteria.
Prohibits public funding programs from using funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety.
Prohibits candidates from using public funds for legal defense costs, fines, or repayment of personal loans to campaigns.
Triples maximum fine for campaign contributions by foreign entities.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs.
FINAL VOTES CAST BY THE LEGISLATURE ON SB 42 (PROPOSITION 4)
(CHAPTER 245, STATUTES OF 2025)

PROP
4
REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 4
YES ON PROPOSITION 4, THE CALIFORNIA FAIR ELECTIONS ACT: ELECTIONS SHOULD BE WON, NOT BOUGHT
The amount of money in California elections is outrageous; it's distorting our democracy. Since 2020, more than $1 billion has been spent on California state candidate races alone. This massive spending gives special interests greater access and influence while drowning out the voices of ordinary Californians.
PROP. 4 HELPS QUALIFIED CANDIDATES COMPETE
Running for office today often requires either personal wealth or access to wealthy donors. Deep pockets have become an unofficial requirement to run for office, leaving too many qualified candidates behind.
PROP. 4 CHANGES THE WAY WE FINANCE ELECTION CAMPAIGNS
Programs like small-dollar donation matching help candidates compete without relying on wealthy donors. However, most California communities are banned from using these tools, allowing the influence of big money to grow.
Proposition 4 lifts that ban, giving voters and local governments the option to adopt public financing with strict safeguards so qualified candidates-regardless of their income-can compete against candidates who are backed by wealthy interests.
PROP. 4 BUILDS ON A PROVEN MODEL
We know this reform works because it's working in other states. Thousands of candidates from different backgrounds have been elected in fourteen states and 26 localities using similar systems. They are new people with good ideas from all walks of life. Because they don't rely on wealthy donors, they can speak their mind and work for the people, not the special interests.
PROP. 4 GIVES LOCAL COMMUNITIES A CHOICE
Proposition 4 does not create a public financing program. It simply gives local governments the option to adopt one if they choose.
If a community does, the cost is as little as $1 per resident each year-a small investment to help counter the billions spent influencing California's elections.
PROP. 4 PROTECTS TAXPAYERS
Taxpayer Safeguards:
Requires candidates to meet strict eligibility criteria and abide by spending limits to qualify for public funds.
Prohibits public funding from favoring incumbents or discriminating based on political party.
Prohibits the use of public funds for legal defense or fines.
PROP. 4 CRACKS DOWN ON ILLEGAL FOREIGN MONEY
Proposition 4 triples the maximum fines for illegal foreign campaign contributions and expenditures, strengthening penalties for those who attempt to interfere in California's elections.
PROP. 4 IS SUPPORTED BY LEADERS ACROSS CALIFORNIA
Proposition 4 is backed by a broad coalition including League of Women Voters of California, California Nurses Association, Mental Health Advocacy Services, Social Security Works, California Clean Money Campaign, California Common Cause, California National Organization for Women, Californians for Disability Rights, Consumer Watchdog, Courage California, Democracy for America, Indivisible California: Statestrong, La Defensa, Money Out Voters In, Voters Right to Know, and many others.
PROP. 4 GIVES CALIFORNIANS THE OPPORTUNITY TO RECLAIM THEIR ELECTIONS and ensure they reflect the values of the people, not just the wealthiest donors.
YES ON 4-Restore power to voters, not wealthy donors
Lorrel Plimier , Co-President
League of Women Voters of California
Catherine Kennedy , President
California Nurses Association
Tom Umberg , California State Senator
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 4
Here is what the politicians supporting Proposition 4 do not tell you:
Proposition 4 REPEALS the voter-approved law that PROHIBITS candidates from using taxpayer money to run for office.
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money. In the election last June, more than 60 candidates ran for Governor. Proposition 4 would allow thousands of candidates to get taxpayer money!
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money a candidate can get. Proposition 4 opens the door to taxpayer-funded campaigns but provides no limits on how much taxpayer money a candidate can get and NO LIMIT on spending. It will lead to more negative ads, more junk mail, and more annoying text messages.
Proposition 4 does NOT PROHIBIT SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY in campaigns. Proposition 4 ALLOWS candidates to get taxpayer money AND to get special interest money! Where exactly is the money going to come from to fund thousands of political campaigns? Proposition 4 does not say. But you know the answer. It is coming from YOU, the taxpayers! Less money for schools, less money for public safety, less money for healthcare. More money for politicians.
Proposition 4 is a BLANK CHECK. It is based on false promises and failed solutions.
Proposition 4 does NOT protect taxpayers. That is why Proposition 4 is opposed by California's leading taxpayer organizations.
Proposition 4 does NOT provide for “fair elections.” That is why Proposition 4 is opposed by former Commissioners of the Fair Political Practices Commission.
Vote NO ON PROPOSITION 4.
Robert Gutierrez , President
California Taxpayers Association
Jon Coupal , President
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association
Dan Schnur , Former Chair
Fair Political Practices Commission
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 4
Why did Sacramento politicians put Proposition 4 on the ballot? They want access to YOUR TAXPAYER MONEY to fund THEIR OWN CAMPAIGNS.
Proposition 4 repeals a voter approved law that PROHIBITS these politicians from using public taxpayer funds for their own campaigns. That's right, Proposition 4 allows politicians to use your taxpayer money to fund their campaigns.
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much money they can get! Proposition 4 is a BLANK CHECK. There isn't even a limit on how much they can spend on their campaigns! More negative ads. More junk mail. More annoying text messages. More, more, more.
Proposition 4 is so poorly written, it could allow every state or local “candidate” to get public funding. They don't even have to actually qualify for the ballot to get taxpayer money. Proposition 4 allows for public funding of thousands of state and local candidates. It even allows for public financing of candidates for county political party committees.
In just the last primary election, there were more than 60 candidates for Governor. Do you want YOUR TAXPAYER MONEY going to support more of their negative campaign ads and junk mail?
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money a candidate can receive. It says it requires “strict criteria” to receive taxpayer funds but provides NO DETAILS on what the criteria are! Read the fine print:
“‘Strict criteria' means the requirement set by statute, ordinance, or charter that candidates must meet to receive public funds.”
But there is no current statute, ordinance or charter setting any criteria. Guess who will be setting the criteria? The same politicians who want to get your taxpayer money!
Some good government groups support public financing of campaigns because they want to get special interest money out of politics. BUT PROPOSITION 4 DOES NOT GET RID OF SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY! Under Proposition 4, candidates can raise money from special interests AND get public funding too.
Proposition 4 is the worst kind of public financing scheme. It provides no specifics. It leaves all the details to be worked out by the same politicians who want to get access to public funds.
It is a blank check. But worse than that, Proposition 4 allows special-interest funding of political campaigns.
Please join California's leading taxpayer protection organizations, including the California Taxpayers Association, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California, United Latinos Action, as well as former members of California's Fair Political Practices Commission, who all oppose Proposition 4.
PLEASE VOTE NO ON THE POLITICIANS' BLANK CHECK PROPOSITION. VOTE NO ON PROP. 4.
Dan Schnur , Former Chair
Fair Political Practices Commission
Colleen McAndrews , Former Commissioner
Fair Political Practices Commission
Julian Canete , President
California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 4
DON'T BE MISLED BY SPECIAL INTERESTS WHO WANT TO KEEP BUYING ELECTIONS
California is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns. Communities in all 49 other states have the right to adopt public financing to allow qualified candidates to compete against wealthy donors. California doesn't. Prop. 4 simply removes that ban and gives local voters the same choice everyone else has, while instituting strict taxpayer safeguards.
PROP. 4 GIVES POWER BACK TO LOCAL COMMUNITIES AND EMPOWERS VOTERS, NOT DONORS
Prop. 4 doesn't spend a single taxpayer dollar or institute public financing anywhere. It simply removes the ban to give every city, county, and the state the right to adopt public funding if local voters want it. The details are appropriately left to each community. But any system MUST require candidates to abide by spending limits and demonstrate broad-based support in their district to qualify.
PROP. 4 MAKES ELECTED OFFICIALS ACCOUNTABLE TO VOTERS, NOT DONORS
Corporate special interests oppose Prop. 4 because public financing allows candidates to run and win without relying on them-threatening their grip on California elections.
Thousands of candidates from different backgrounds have been elected across the country using public financing, for a tiny cost. Because they don't rely on wealthy donors, they can speak their minds and work for the people, not special interests.
DON'T BE FOOLED BY CORPORATE SPECIAL INTERESTS HIDING BEHIND NICE-SOUNDING NAMES.
VOTE YES ON 4 to let local voters and communities reclaim their elections so they're won, not bought.
Carmen Balber , Executive Director
Consumer Watchdog
Camerina Davidson , President
California National Organization for Women
Darius Kemp , Executive Director
California Common Cause

PROP
4
REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
The Political Reform Act. Many people, groups, and businesses spend money to support or oppose candidates for public office and ballot measures. California's Political Reform Act sets rules for how money can be used in politics and requires public reporting of political spending. These rules apply to state and local candidates, ballot measures, and other public officials, but not to federal candidates or officials. (Federal law establishes campaign finance and reporting requirements for federal offices.) The Political Reform Act has been updated by voters over the years.
Ban on Public Funds to Pay for Campaigns. The Political Reform Act bans the use of public funds for political candidates' campaigns. This ban applies to most elected offices at the state level and local level. (This ban does not apply to city office elections in certain charter cities. Los Angeles, San Francisco, Long Beach, Oakland, and Berkeley are current examples of charter cities that provide public funds to certain campaigns.)
Entities That Oversee Campaign Finance Laws. California's campaign finance laws are administered by the Fair Political Practices Commission and the California Secretary of State. State law requires people and groups to report how much money they give, receive, and spend on political campaigns. This information is available to the public on the Secretary of State's website. The Fair Political Practices Commission enforces and interprets the Political Reform Act. The Fair Political Practices Commission reviews the finance reports and can fine candidates and donors who break the law. The Fair Political Practices Commission issues guidance based on its interpretation of the Political Reform Act.
PROPOSAL
Lifts Ban on Use of Public Funds to Pay for Candidates' Campaigns. Proposition 4 lifts the ban on using public funds for political candidates' campaigns. Removing the ban allows state and local governments to create public campaign financing programs in the future if they wish. Proposition 4 does not create a public campaign finance system for the state or local governments directly.
Sets Rules for Future State and Local Public Campaign Finance Programs. Proposition 4 sets broad rules for future state and local public campaign finance programs but leaves many key design decisions to future state and local decision makers. Proposition 4 limits which public funds can be used for campaigns, who can receive the funds, and how the funds can be spent in any future public campaign finance program. For example, money meant for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used for campaigns. Candidates can only receive public funds if they show broad-based support in their district and agree to spending limits and other program rules. Public funds cannot be used for legal defense fees or fines, or to repay a candidate's personal campaign loan. State and local governments can design and implement their own programs within the broad rules set by Proposition 4.
Fair Political Practices Commission Would Issue Guidance on Public Campaign Finance Programs. Proposition 4 specifies that the Fair Political Practices Commission is not required to administer or enforce local public campaign finance programs. Rather, state and local government officials could ask the Fair Political Practices Commission for guidance on how to create public campaign finance programs consistent with Proposition 4.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Costs of Possible Public Campaign Finance Programs Depend on Future Decisions. Proposition 4 does not create a public campaign finance program. However, it allows state and local governments to create such programs in the future. The cost of these programs could be significant for governments that choose to create them. The total cost would depend on which governments created such programs and how those programs were designed.
Minor State Costs to Support State and Local Governments Considering Public Campaign Finance Programs. If voters approve Proposition 4, state and local government officials likely would ask the Fair Political Practices Commission for guidance on creating public campaign finance programs under the Political Reform Act. This likely would require the Fair Political Practices Commission to hire more legal staff to help answer these questions. As a result, state costs would be a few hundred thousand dollars each year. This amount is much less than one-tenth of 1 percent (0.1 percent) of the state's total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)

California (https://berkeleypoliticalreview.org/category/california/) Our Guide to the 2026 California Ballot Propositions
By Caspar Turner & Molly Urfalian (https://berkeleypoliticalreview.org/author/eics/) · October 23, 2026
There are fourteen statewide propositions in California this year; the following are our recommendations on how you should cast your vote. Researching every proposition can be arduous, which is why we made this guide. We will provide a brief description of each proposition, a “yes” or “no” recommendation, and the reasoning behind our position. The deadline to vote in the 2026 midterm elections is Tuesday, November 3rd.
Proposition 1: YES
Affordable housing doesn’t pay for itself, but this proposition would help fund it.
Prop. 1 would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds: $10 billion for general affordable housing and $1.25 billion for veterans’ housing.
Funds from California’s 2018 housing bond have all been spent. The costs of this bond will be dispersed over a period of twenty-five years and will help our state’s most vulnerable populations. No formal arguments were filed against this proposition — only the infamously avaricious Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association objects (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/) to it.
Proposition 2: YES
The economic future of our state is not certain. This proposition would help us protect it.
Prop. 2 would double California’s existing Rainy Day Fund (which was approved (https://vigarchive.sos.ca.gov/2014/general/en/propositions/2/) by CA voters 12 years ago). The fund’s cap would be increased from 10% to 20% of the state budget, and the measure would mandate larger deposits during economic upturns.
Trump often attacks California rhetorically, even going as far as to state that the two biggest cities in the state would be no great loss (https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c6r7yn8pknyxo) if destroyed in a war. This should be taken seriously, even if he claims it to be a joke. California should future-proof itself.
Partisan politics aside, saving more is often an economically sound decision. If we grow the Rainy Day Fund even further, we can prepare for the next recession. California’s revenue need not determine our quality of life.
Proposition 3: YES
Letting our income tax rates expire would cost California up to $15 billion (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/quick-reference-guide/3.htm) a year just to give tax cuts to high earners. This proposition would prevent that.
Prop. 3 would maintain existing tax rates on Californians earning more than $371,000 (the top 2% of earners in the state), and allocate tax revenue to public education and healthcare. Various taxpayers’ associations might try to label this a tax increase, but it would just mean a continuation of the status quo. When our state has higher income inequality (https://www.ppic.org/publication/income-inequality-in-california/) than the rest of the nation on average, do we really need to focus on relieving millionaires? Might we not better spend our energy helping our underfunded public schools and hospitals?
Proposition 4: YES
Elections should be won rather than bought. This proposition would be a step in the right direction.
Prop. 4 would reverse California’s ban on public campaign finance programs. CA is currently the only state in the entire country that has a blanket ban on this type of public funding. As a result, statewide and (most) local elections can be conducted only with support from private donors. This effectively makes politics a “pay-to-win” system in which gubernatorial candidates have spent (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/11/opinion/tom-steyer-california-governor.html) up to $216 million in primary elections alone.
There is an alternative to this. Berkeley — as a charter city — is exempt from the ban on public campaign financing. Candidates for mayor and city council in Berkeley become eligible for the Public Financing Program (https://berkeleyca.gov/sites/default/files/documents/Public%20Financing%20Program%20Guide%202024%20-%20FINAL_1.pdf) if they agree to take no individual donation larger than $60. If they opt into the program, they receive six dollars in public funds for every dollar they raise from Berkeley residents.
This program has worked to reduce money’s influence in Berkeley’s politics. In the first election cycle after the enactment of the PFP, contributions from non-Berkeley residents dropped from 33% to 10% (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/major-strides-public-campaign-financing). City residents have become more influential in their own elections.
Expanding this model seems like a good idea to us. Democracy is never perfectly formed initially. We must continually strive toward more fairness in elections, and Prop. 4 is a good place to start.
Proposition 5: YES
Recall elections should be just that — recalls. This proposition would ensure that.
Prop. 5 would establish (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/) a new type of election in California. Under current state law, recall ballots ask two questions: whether or not the government official in question should be removed, and who should replace them. It is perfectly legal for a voter to fill in their ballot for the first question while ignoring the second. Prop. 5 would limit recalls to asking the first question, and put the second question to an appointment or a separate election.
The problem with the current two-question system of recall elections is that only a specific subset of voters participates in recalls. Those who oppose a current incumbent are more likely to vote in recalls, and this currently means they also get a larger say in who the replacement official ends up being. In 2003, Arnold Schwarzenegger won the governorship through a recall, despite being a Republican in a predominantly Democratic state. His widespread name recognition as a movie star likely aided greatly in this.
That brings us to another problem with the current system. Because potential replacement candidates don’t have time to campaign properly during a recall election (and may not even know if a recall will be successful), name recognition is simply too powerful in these bundled elections. Moving the process of picking a replacement candidate to a separate election would be fairer to less well-known candidates.
While it could potentially cost the state a few million dollars in the event of a recall, these special elections are rare and controversial events. Getting them right, and making it less likely that candidates who don’t represent the California electorate’s views get elected, seems important enough to pay for.
Proposition 37: YES
Homeownership should be incentivized, especially if it won’t cost us anything. This proposition is an obvious “yes” vote.
Prop. 37 would let (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/37/) the state sell $25 billion worth of bonds to pay for middle-class Californians to get mortgages on certain types of homes. These homebuyers must choose to live in these houses, as well as pay at least 3% down. The official California Voter Information Guide itself characterizes this proposition as having no “direct state or local costs” at all. We see no reason not to vote for it (no opponent even submitted an argument against this proposition on the Voter Information Guide).
Proposition 38: YES
The Trump administration has been systematically targeting scientific research by cutting (https://www.sciencenews.org/article/nih-nsf-cuts-2025-data) at least $3 billion of funding. This proposition would help mitigate the impact on crucial California research initiatives.
Prop. 38 would authorize (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/) $8.4 billion worth of funding for immunology and immunotherapy research. About $4.2 billion of this would almost certainly go (https://growsf.org/news/2026-07-02-14-state-measures/) to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, while the rest would fund research grants throughout the state. While the fact that this Institute’s founder is the primary bankroller of Prop. 38 may seem to reek of corruption, the benefits of this proposition still outweigh the costs.
Like Prop. 1, Prop. 38 would cost California hundreds of millions of dollars a year to pay off its debt, and like Prop. 1, these costs would be distributed over two decades. Alzheimer’s, heart disease, and cancer take millions of lives every year. Innovating solutions for them will help the entire world, not just Californian scientists.
Proposition 39: NO
Pushes to change Voter ID laws are politicized attacks on our democracy. They should be voted down.
Prop. 39 would require (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/) Voter ID at polling stations and, more significantly, would require all mail-in ballots (which 90% of Californians (https://calvoter.org/content/should-you-use-usps-mail-your-midterm-ballot-here%E2%80%99s-what-california-election-officials-say) use to vote) to be marked with the last four digits of a government ID number. It is an unnecessary concession to unsubstantiated and constant (https://abcnews.com/Politics/timeline-donald-trumps-election-denial-claims-republican-politicians/story?id=89168408) Republican claims of widespread mail voting fraud (which only occurs (https://www.brookings.edu/articles/mail-voting-in-the-us-data-points-to-very-low-fraud-and-significant-benefits-to-voters/) in roughly four of every 10 million ballots cast), and could be used to throw out millions of ballots. Voter ID is already required to register as a voter in California. All this proposition does is create another way for voters’ ballots to be thrown out in a state where almost 100,000 valid ballots were rejected (https://calvoter.org/content/making-sense-150000-rejected-california-mail-ballots) for arriving late in this year’s primary alone.
With a lawbreaking Riverside County sheriff and Republican gubernatorial candidate seizing ballots (https://berkeleypoliticalreview.org/2026/05/20/voting-rights-are-under-attack-california-must-stand-up-and-fight-back/) earlier this year, the last thing we need is to modify voting in this state. As usual, the only organizations on the “wrong side” of this proposition are the taxpayers’ associations. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association is in favor (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/) of this proposition passing because it would “secure” elections (i.e., make it harder to vote). This is fundamentally anti-democratic and should be opposed.
The “Billionaire Tax” Propositions:
YES on 40, NO on 41, NO on 42
These 3 propositions, which were put on the ballot by petition, are tied together. Prop. 40, possibly the most controversial (https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/californias-billionaire-tax-faces-mountain-opposition-not-just-rich-rcna604397) proposition of this election, would impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of California’s ~255 billionaires. Collectively, these high-wealth individuals hold over $2 trillion (https://www.oxfamamerica.org/explore/research-publications/billionaire-wealth-in-california/) (that’s two million millions) in total net worth.
Billionaires have fought tooth and nail to try to defeat Prop. 40. Mark Zuckerberg — perhaps California’s most iconic billionaire — has threatened to leave (https://www.bizjournals.com/sanfrancisco/news/2026/10/21/mark-zuckerberg-relocate-california-prop-40.html) the state if it passes. One might very well take this as an indication that Prop. 40 would be effective. And even if billionaires leave now, they will still have to pay the tax. Prop. 40 applies to anyone who was a California resident on January 1st (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-40) of this year.
The Voter Information Guide (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/quick-reference-guide/40.htm) says that Prop. 40 would raise tens of billions of dollars over several years, and that potential losses of income tax from billionaires relocating are estimated at less than $1 billion a year. This would be a net positive in terms of funds that would go to finance our streets, our schools, and our hospitals.
Even if Prop. 40 passes — as polling suggests (https://calmatters.org/newsletter/billionaire-tax-proposition-poll/) it might — Propositions 41 and 42 are aimed at undoing it. If either passes with more “yes” votes than Prop. 40, they will nullify its effects. Prop. 41 would nullify any new tax that exempts its revenue from California’s state spending limit (as the wealth tax proposed by Prop. 40 would). Prop. 42 would outright ban any wealth taxes in the state constitution.
Both of these reactionary propositions were funded by an organization that calls itself “Building a Better California” — which derives over half of its revenue (https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/29/politics/sergey-brin-california-wealth-tax) from Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who was willing to shell out $100 million from his quarter-trillion-dollar fortune in order to avoid paying a $14 billion tax.
Studies have suggested (https://www.cnbc.com/make-it/2018/01/03/harvard-study-how-much-money-millionaires-need-to-be-happy.html) that human happiness maxes out at around an $8 million net worth. Perhaps any more than this only has negative repercussions on one’s personality.
Sergey Brin can afford to pay his fair share in order to support the state that facilitated his success. So can the rest of the over 250 billionaires that made their fortunes in California. Vote yes on Prop. 40, and no on Propositions 41 and 42.
Proposition 43: NO
This is an anti-democratic measure posing as fiscal responsibility. It should be opposed.
Prop. 43, very succinctly, would allow (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/) ⅓ of voters to veto the decisions of a ⅔ majority. Historically, special taxes in California have been able to pass with a simple majority (if they are proposed by citizens’ initiative rather than by city council members). These local measures are important for funding public transit, wildfire protection programs, and housing development.
The money-obsessed members of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association would like nothing more than to make these crucial taxes harder to pass, which is why (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/) they authored this proposition. Firefighters, teachers, and nurses all oppose Prop. 43. You should too.
Proposition 44: NO
While it may seem reasonable at first, this proposition is too extreme a solution for the problem it seems to combat. It should be voted against.
Prop. 44 would fine any community health clinic (a type of nonprofit health center) that spends less than 90% of its revenue on “program services” (direct clinical expenditures, as opposed to management and technology costs). Currently, clinics spend an average (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/analysis.htm) of about 80% of their revenue on these services. If Prop. 44 passes, they would be required to pay exorbitant penalties, and, according to the California Primary Care Association, more than half may be forced (https://calmatters.org/newsletter/prop-44-medical-clinics/) to close. Disproportionately, community health clinics serve low-income and rural communities. This proposition passing would hurt members of these communities more than anyone else.
The labor union SEIU-UHW (Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West) is the main backer of Prop. 44. Most of SEIU-UHW’s members work at hospitals, not community clinics. The clinics potentially affected by Prop. 44 are largely non-union, and a coalition of them has alleged (https://www.legalnewsline.com/northern-california-record/union-uses-ca-ballot-initiatives-to-strongarm-clinics-lawsuit/article_7c623996-6763-48fc-88bf-65d50af60749.html) in a lawsuit that Prop. 44 serves as a bargaining chip for SEIU-UHW. They claim that the union offered to drop the proposition if union membership at community clinics increased.
Voting in favor of Prop. 44 is not in the public interest. There is a reason this proposition is opposed by Democrats and Republicans alike, as well as (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/) the California Medical Association. You should vote “no” on it.
Proposition 45: NO
YIMBY (“Yes In My Backyard”) groups are largely not in favor of this seemingly progressive ballot measure. That’s one indicator that voting for it might not be a wise choice.
Prop. 45 would accelerate (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/) the timeline for environmental review of “essential” developments like housing and “broadband internet access” infrastructure, as well as require California courts to rule on California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) cases within 270 days (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-45-environmental-review/).
A State Assembly bill written by housing-forward Assemblymember Buffy Wicks that streamlined CEQA was enacted (https://www.venable.com/insights/publications/2025/07/from-red-tape-to-green-light-ceqa-reforms-fast) last year (alongside a similar State Senate bill). But California YIMBY, which helped to write these reforms, declines to support (https://hoodline.com/2026/10/six-california-gop-county-committees-recommend-no-on-prop-45/) Prop. 45. It was placed on the ballot by the pro-business California Chamber of Commerce to “cut unnecessary delays” (https://advocacy.calchamber.com/alert/2026/07/voters-strongly-support-calchambers-prop-45) on development, while its opponents include the Coalition for Clean Air and CA Environmental Voters. Fundamentally, Prop. 45 is more than just a pro-housing measure. It could increase the likelihood (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/07/proposition-45-environment-health-protections/) of pollution in certain communities because it encourages rapid development, and its classification of “broadband internet access” development as being “essential” could fast-track data center construction, which 61% of Americans oppose (https://www.annenbergpublicpolicycenter.org/opposition-to-local-data-centers-rises-sharply-annenberg-survey-finds/). You should oppose this proposition as well.
Conclusion
Of these fourteen propositions, the five most crucial ones to vote on (3, 40, 41, 42, and 43) all center around the extent to which money should be able to buy influence in politics. Supporting 3 and 40 — and opposing 41, 42, and 43 — is the sensible position for those of us who believe in popular democracy; in fair, majority-wins elections; and in increased funding for our increasingly left-behind public schools and healthcare systems.

By Molly Urfalian · May 2, 2025
My phone was constantly buzzing with “Breaking News” alerts during the first day of Trump’s presidency.
Seeing the flood of his executive orders, withdrawing the U.S. from the Paris Climate Agreement, the World Health Organization, eliminating DEI programs, and more was exhausting.
But I caught a break when I saw the headline reading “Trump renames ‘Gulf of Mexico’ to ‘Gulf of America’”.
...
After the initial shock faded, I had to ask: besides the fact that this was a hilarious move, why did he do it?
Well, he did not just rename the Gulf of Mexico; he has renamed a few geographical places around America.
Renaming the Gulf and “Mount Denali” is part of Trump’s Executive Order, “Restoring Names that Honor American Greatness.”
Unpacking these seemingly irrelevant changes and a few other examples reveals some patterns in Trump’s renaming frenzy.

# Proposition 4
Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns.
Legislative Statute.
## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
***Lifts Ban on Use of Public Funds to Pay for Candidates’ Campaigns.*** Proposition 4 lifts the ban on using public funds for political candidates’ campaigns.
Removing the ban allows state and local governments to create public campaign financing programs in the future if they wish.
Proposition 4 does not create a public campaign finance system for the state or local governments directly.
...
## Yes/No Statement
A **YES** vote on this measure means: State and local governments could create public campaign financing programs for public office candidates, subject to limits on which public funds could be used, how the public funds could be used, and who could receive them.
A **NO** vote on this measure means: State and most local governments would remain unable to create public campaign finance programs for public office candidates.

  * Prohibits using public campaign funds for fines, legal defense, or repayment of personal candidate loans.
  * Triples maximum fines for illegal campaign contributions from foreign entities.

As an AI assistant, I cannot tell you how to vote or make voting decisions on your behalf, which is why I cannot provide a simple "yes" or "no" answer. How you should vote on **Proposition 4** (the California Fair Elections Act) is a personal choice that depends on your values, priorities, and perspective on campaign finance and government spending.

Below is an objective overview of the measure, what each vote means, and the primary arguments from both supporters and opponents to help inform your decision.

---

### What Proposition 4 Does

Proposition 4 amends California's Political Reform Act of 1974 to **repeal the existing ban on state and local governments offering public funding for political campaigns**. 

* **Current Law:** Since 1988 (following Proposition 73), California law has prohibited the use of public funds for political candidate campaigns, except in charter cities and counties that have established their own systems (such as Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Berkeley).
* **Proposed Law:** Prop 4 lifts that statewide ban, allowing state and local governments the option to establish public campaign financing programs. It does not automatically create a statewide funding system or mandate that local governments create one; rather, it permits them to do so under specific statutory guidelines.
* **Key Provisions & Safeguards:**
  * Prohibits using public funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety.
  * Requires participating candidates to meet strict eligibility requirements (demonstrating broad community support through small-dollar contributions) and agree to expenditure limits.
  * Prohibits using public campaign funds for fines, legal defense, or repayment of personal candidate loans.
  * Triples maximum fines for illegal campaign contributions from foreign entities.

---

### What Your Vote Means

* **A YES vote means:** State and local governments would be authorized to establish public campaign financing programs for candidates who meet qualification requirements and agree to spending limits.
* **A NO vote means:** The statewide ban remains in place; state and most local governments would continue to be prohibited from creating public campaign financing programs.

---

### Arguments in Favor (Voting YES)

* **Curbing the Influence of Big Donors:** Proponents argue that political campaigns in California are increasingly dominated by wealthy donors and special interest PACs. Public financing (such as small-dollar donation matching) allows candidates without access to personal wealth or big-dollar networks to run competitive campaigns.
* **Encouraging Grassroots Candidates and Diversity:** Supporters point to models in charter cities (e.g., Berkeley, San Francisco) and other states where public financing has helped a broader, more diverse pool of candidates enter politics and engage with local constituents rather than large financial backers.
* **Taxpayer Protections:** The measure includes explicit restrictions preventing funds from being drawn from education, roads, or public safety budgets, and sets rules to prevent candidates from using funds for personal enrichment or legal fees.
* **Local Control:** Supporters emphasize that the measure does not mandate spending; it gives local communities the democratic choice to adopt public financing if they determine it benefits their governance.

*Key Supporters include:* League of Women Voters of California, California Common Cause, California Clean Money Campaign, Consumer Watchdog, California Nurses Association, and various civic advocacy groups.

---

### Arguments Against (Voting NO)

* **Use of Taxpayer Dollars for Politics:** Opponents argue that taxpayer money should be reserved for essential public services and infrastructure rather than subsidizing political careers, negative campaign commercials, junk mail, and campaign consultants.
* **Lack of Specific Limits in the Text:** Critics contend the proposition creates a framework but leaves the specific funding mechanisms, candidate qualification thresholds, and total spending amounts to be determined by future legislation or the politicians themselves.
* **Does Not Stop Special Interest Spending:** Opponents point out that public funding does not eliminate independent expenditure committees (Super PACs) or outside political spending, meaning taxpayer money could simply be added on top of existing private and special interest money.
* **Fiscal Burden:** In times of state or local budget deficits, opponents maintain that even modest administrative and program costs are an unnecessary use of public revenue.

*Key Opponents include:* California Taxpayers Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association of California, United Latinos Action, and former members of the Fair Political Practices Commission.

---

### Conclusion

* If you believe that allowing public financing is an effective way to level the playing field, reduce reliance on wealthy donors, and give everyday voters a stronger voice in elections, you may lean toward voting **YES**.
* If you believe that public taxpayer dollars should never be used to finance political campaigns, or that public financing systems are ineffective and open to misuse by politicians, you may lean toward voting **NO**.

As an AI assistant, I cannot tell you how to vote or make voting decisions on your behalf, which is why I cannot provide a simple "yes" or "no" answer. How you should vote on **Proposition 4** (the California Fair Elections Act) is a personal choice that depends on your values, priorities, and perspective on campaign finance and government spending.

Below is an objective overview of the measure, what each vote means, and the primary arguments from both supporters and opponents to help inform your decision.

---

### What Proposition 4 Does

Proposition 4 amends California's Political Reform Act of 1974 to **repeal the existing ban on state and local governments offering public funding for political campaigns**. 

* **Current Law:** Since 1988 (following Proposition 73), California law has prohibited the use of public funds for political candidate campaigns, except in charter cities and counties that have established their own systems (such as Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Berkeley).
* **Proposed Law:** Prop 4 lifts that statewide ban, allowing state and local governments the option to establish public campaign financing programs. It does not automatically create a statewide funding system or mandate that local governments create one; rather, it permits them to do so under specific statutory guidelines.
* **Key Provisions & Safeguards:**
  * Prohibits using public funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety.
  * Requires participating candidates to meet strict eligibility requirements (demonstrating broad community support through small-dollar contributions) and agree to expenditure limits.
  * Prohibits using public campaign funds for fines, legal defense, or repayment of personal candidate loans.
  * Triples maximum fines for illegal campaign contributions from foreign entities.

---

### What Your Vote Means

* **A YES vote means:** State and local governments would be authorized to establish public campaign financing programs for candidates who meet qualification requirements and agree to spending limits.
* **A NO vote means:** The statewide ban remains in place; state and most local governments would continue to be prohibited from creating public campaign financing programs.

---

### Arguments in Favor (Voting YES)

* **Curbing the Influence of Big Donors:** Proponents argue that political campaigns in California are increasingly dominated by wealthy donors and special interest PACs. Public financing (such as small-dollar donation matching) allows candidates without access to personal wealth or big-dollar networks to run competitive campaigns.
* **Encouraging Grassroots Candidates and Diversity:** Supporters point to models in charter cities (e.g., Berkeley, San Francisco) and other states where public financing has helped a broader, more diverse pool of candidates enter politics and engage with local constituents rather than large financial backers.
* **Taxpayer Protections:** The measure includes explicit restrictions preventing funds from being drawn from education, roads, or public safety budgets, and sets rules to prevent candidates from using funds for personal enrichment or legal fees.
* **Local Control:** Supporters emphasize that the measure does not mandate spending; it gives local communities the democratic choice to adopt public financing if they determine it benefits their governance.

*Key Supporters include:* League of Women Voters of California, California Common Cause, California Clean Money Campaign, Consumer Watchdog, California Nurses Association, and various civic advocacy groups.

---

### Arguments Against (Voting NO)

* **Use of Taxpayer Dollars for Politics:** Opponents argue that taxpayer money should be reserved for essential public services and infrastructure rather than subsidizing political careers, negative campaign commercials, junk mail, and campaign consultants.
* **Lack of Specific Limits in the Text:** Critics contend the proposition creates a framework but leaves the specific funding mechanisms, candidate qualification thresholds, and total spending amounts to be determined by future legislation or the politicians themselves.
* **Does Not Stop Special Interest Spending:** Opponents point out that public funding does not eliminate independent expenditure committees (Super PACs) or outside political spending, meaning taxpayer money could simply be added on top of existing private and special interest money.
* **Fiscal Burden:** In times of state or local budget deficits, opponents maintain that even modest administrative and program costs are an unnecessary use of public revenue.

*Key Opponents include:* California Taxpayers Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association of California, United Latinos Action, and former members of the Fair Political Practices Commission.

---

### Conclusion

* If you believe that allowing public financing is an effective way to level the playing field, reduce reliance on wealthy donors, and give everyday voters a stronger voice in elections, you may lean toward voting **YES**.
* If you believe that public taxpayer dollars should never be used to finance political campaigns, or that public financing systems are ineffective and open to misuse by politicians, you may lean toward voting **NO**.
